Electronic Sensors
Vibration Analysis Questions and Answers on Sensors, Units, ISO Zones, FFT and Fault Frequencies

These are the questions interviewers and exam papers ask most about machine vibration, grouped by topic with short, checkable answers. Every formula comes with a worked number you can repeat in the calculator or on a site walkdown.

Accelerometer vs Probe mm/s, µm and g ISO 10816 Zones FFT and Fmax Bearing Frequencies

A topic wise set of vibration analysis questions and answers covering sensors, units, ISO severity zones, FFT settings and fault signatures. It includes a unit conversion calculator, a sampling example and a solved bearing frequency example.

Hello everyone, today we are going to work through the vibration analysis questions and answers that come up most in instrumentation and maintenance interviews, with numbers you can check yourself.
Quick Answer

What are the most important vibration analysis questions and answers for interviews?

Vibration analysis questions and answers mostly test sensor choice, units, severity limits, FFT settings and fault signatures. The key formula: velocity peak equals 2πf times displacement peak, and acceleration peak equals 2πf times velocity peak. For example, 4.5 mm/s rms at 25 Hz equals 81 µm peak to peak and 0.102 g peak, the C to D boundary for an ISO 10816 group 2 machine on a rigid foundation.

What Is Vibration Analysis in Condition Monitoring?

Vibration analysis is the measurement of machine vibration amplitude and frequency to find faults such as unbalance, misalignment, looseness and bearing wear before they cause a breakdown. These vibration analysis questions and answers start from the sensor and end at the spectrum, the same path an analyst follows on site.

Key Facts
  • Three sensors: accelerometer (g), velocity sensor (mm/s) and proximity probe (µm).
  • Casing severity under ISO 10816 and ISO 20816 is judged in mm/s rms.
  • At one frequency, velocity is 2πf times displacement and acceleration is 2πf times velocity.
  • Unbalance shows at 1X, misalignment adds 2X and axial 1X, bearing defects are non synchronous.

If you are new to the hardware, read our vibration sensor working guide first. The companion post on vibration analysis with AI for predictive maintenance shows how the same spectra feed machine learning models.

Sensor Questions: Accelerometer, Velocity Sensor or Proximity Probe?

Use an accelerometer for general casing readings and bearing faults, a velocity sensor for low and medium speed machines, and a proximity probe for shaft motion in sleeve bearings. Most vibration analysis questions and answers on sensors come back to this table.

QuestionAccelerometerVelocity sensorProximity probe
MeasuresCasing accelerationCasing velocityShaft displacement
Usual unitg peakmm/s rmsµm pk to pk
Sensitivity (Metrix)100 mV/g3.94 mV per mm/s7.87 mV/µm
Strong atMedium and high speedLow and medium speedLow frequency shaft motion
Typical useMotors, pumps, gearboxesFans, slow pumpsTurbines, compressors

How does a piezoelectric accelerometer work? A seismic mass loads a piezoelectric crystal, which produces charge in proportion to acceleration, and an internal IEPE amplifier turns that charge into a voltage on a two wire cable.

The crystal physics is the same as in piezoelectric pressure sensors, so neither measures a static value. Many wireless nodes use a capacitive element instead, which we cover in the MEMS accelerometer working principle post.

Why is an accelerometer a poor choice on a slow machine? Metrix shows that at 600 rpm, 0.5 in/s peak gives only about 8 mV from a 100 mV/g accelerometer but 50 mV from a velocity sensor.

Why are two proximity probes fitted at each bearing? Two probes set 90 degrees apart, usually 45 degrees either side of vertical, give X and Y signals that together show the shaft orbit inside the bearing clearance.

API 670 covers these systems on critical turbines and compressors, while smaller machines often get only a vibration switch for machine protection or a 4 to 20 mA vibration transmitter wired to the DCS.

Do You Know?

Metrix describes a piezo velocity sensor as an accelerometer with an internal integrator. Its output is stronger relative to noise than integrating a raw accelerometer signal in the monitor.

Vibration Units Conversion: How Do You Change mm/s to µm and g?

For a single frequency sine wave, divide velocity by 2πf to get displacement and multiply velocity by 2πf to get acceleration. Convert rms to peak first, because the three units are quoted on different bases.

Which basis goes with which unit? Displacement is usually quoted peak to peak, velocity as rms and acceleration as peak, and for a pure sine the peak is 1.414 times the rms value.

Given: vrms = 4.5 mm/s at f = 25 Hz
ω = 2π × 25 = 157.1 rad/s
vpeak = 4.5 × 1.414 = 6.36 mm/s
dpk to pk = 2 × 6.36 ÷ 157.1
= 0.0810 mm = 81.0 µm
apeak = 157.1 × 6.36 = 1000 mm/s²
= 1.00 m/s² = 0.102 g
Vibration Velocity to Displacement and Acceleration
Equivalent values for a sine at this frequency
Displacement 81.0 µm pk to pk, acceleration 0.102 g peak (1.00 m/s²)
Quick Tip

Run the calculator at 2.5 Hz and at 250 Hz with the same 4.5 mm/s. Displacement falls 100 times and acceleration rises 100 times, which is why each sensor suits a different speed range.

ISO 10816 Vibration Severity Chart: What Are Zones A to D?

ISO 10816 grades a machine by its broadband velocity in mm/s rms on the bearing housing and places it in zone A, B, C or D. ISO 20816 part 3 of 2022 has now replaced ISO 10816 part 3 for industrial machines.

ISO 10816 part 3 (mm/s rms)A/BB/CC/D
Group 1, above 300 kW, rigid2.34.57.1
Group 1, above 300 kW, flexible3.57.111.0
Group 2, 15 to 300 kW, rigid1.42.84.5
Group 2, 15 to 300 kW, flexible2.34.57.1

What do the four zones mean? Zone A is typical of newly commissioned machines, zone B is fine for long term running, zone C is unsatisfactory for continuous running and zone D can cause damage.

The standard measures from 10 to 1000 Hz, or 2 to 1000 Hz below 600 rpm. So 4.5 mm/s on a 90 kW pump motor sits at the C to D line on a concrete block but only at B to C on a flexible frame.

Myth: One ISO number tells you what is wrong.
Fact: The zone grades severity; the spectrum and phase show the cause.
Myth: A reading inside zone B needs no action.
Fact: A steady rise inside zone B is still a warning worth trending.
Myth: ISO casing limits apply to the shaft too.
Fact: Shaft displacement has its own limits in µm from the OEM or ISO 20816.

How Do You Set Up an FFT Spectrum? Sampling, Fmax and Lines

Choose Fmax to cover the highest fault frequency you expect, and enough lines to separate peaks that sit close together. The analyser then sets the sample rate and the time record from those two numbers.

SensorAccelerometer on the housing
ConditioningIEPE supply and anti aliasing filter
ADCSamples at 2.56 times Fmax
WindowHanning window on each block
FFTSpectrum with the chosen lines
AverageSeveral spectra averaged

Why sample at 2.56 times Fmax and not twice? Nyquist sets the minimum at twice the highest frequency, and the extra margin gives the low pass anti aliasing filter room to roll off, and because the analog to digital conversion runs in blocks, 1600 lines use 4096 samples.

Fmax = 1000 Hz, lines = 1600
Resolution = 1000 ÷ 1600 = 0.625 Hz
Sample rate = 2.56 × 1000 = 2560 per second
Block = 2.56 × 1600 = 4096 samples
Time per average = 1600 ÷ 1000 = 1.6 s

Why can doubling the lines make a route slower? At the same Fmax, 3200 lines need 3.2 s per average instead of 1.6 s, yet Brüel and Kjær advise a resolution 5 to 10 times finer than the gap you need to separate.

Fault Questions: What Do 1X, 2X and Harmonics Mean?

1X is the running speed frequency and 2X is twice running speed, and the pattern of these orders points to the fault. The four cases below cover most spectrum reading questions.

Unbalance

High radial 1X, low axial vibration, steady phase.

Best for: Fans, impellers
1X radial
Misalignment

High axial 1X or strong 2X, phase shift across the coupling.

Best for: Motor pump sets
1X axial, 2X
Looseness

A long row of 1X harmonics, sometimes with half order peaks.

Best for: Baseplates, soft foot
Harmonics
Bearing defect

Non synchronous peaks such as BPFO and BPFI.

Best for: Ball bearing machines
BPFO, BPFI

Why is the 1X peak of a 1500 rpm motor not exactly at 25 Hz? A 4 pole motor on a 50 Hz supply runs a little below 1500 rpm because of induction motor slip, so its 1X peak sits slightly under 25 Hz.

Fluke lists unbalance, looseness, misalignment and bearing degradation as the four most common machine faults. The flowchart below sorts them from the dominant peaks.

Do You Know?

Fluke splits looseness into three types: type A at the feet, baseplate or foundation, type B from loose fasteners or cracked frames, and type C from improper fits and wear.

How Are Bearing Defect Frequencies Calculated?

Bearing defect frequencies come from the number of rolling elements, the ball and pitch diameters, the contact angle and shaft speed. Each is a fixed multiple of running speed, so you can mark them in advance.

BPFO = (n ÷ 2) × fr × (1 minus (d ÷ D) cos θ)
BPFI = (n ÷ 2) × fr × (1 + (d ÷ D) cos θ)
6205: n = 9, d = 7.94 mm, D = 39.04 mm, θ = 0
d ÷ D = 0.2034, fr = 25 Hz
BPFO = 4.5 × 25 × 0.7966 = 89.6 Hz
BPFI = 4.5 × 25 × 1.2034 = 135.4 Hz

Why are bearing peaks called non synchronous? Their multiples of running speed, 3.58X and 5.42X for the 6205, are not whole numbers, so they never line up with 1X harmonics.

Metrix notes that bearing defects show from about 1 to 6 times BPFO, which sets the minimum Fmax for a bearing route. On VFD driven motors, also rule out VFD motor bearing currents, which damage the races and then show the same peaks.

Quick Tip

For early bearing damage, Brüel and Kjær use envelope analysis: band pass the signal around a high frequency resonance, demodulate it and take the FFT of the envelope. BPFO and BPFI then stand out clearly.

Mounting and Field Questions: Why Do Readings Change?

Readings change mostly because the sensor was mounted differently, placed elsewhere or the load changed.

Which accelerometer mounting gives the widest frequency range? PCB Piezotronics states that a stud on a smooth, flat surface gives the broadest range, while easy mount clips can drop the upper limit to about 1 to 3.5 kHz.

  • Mark each point so every route reading is taken at the same spot.
  • Clean the surface and apply a thin layer of silicone grease, as PCB advises.
  • For a permanent adhesive mount, use two part epoxy.
  • Record speed and load with each reading.
Online monitoring strengths
  • Continuous data catches faults between route visits.
  • Stud mounted sensors give repeatable readings.
  • Alarms and trips can go through the DCS.
Online monitoring limits
  • Higher cost per point.
  • Someone still has to review the alarms.
  • Covers only the points chosen at design time.

Most plants put online systems on critical trains and handheld routes on the rest, a choice covered in our article on predictive and preventive maintenance. Weak signals on slow machines are a noise problem, and our signal to noise ratio calculator helps size that margin.

Vibration Analysis Questions and Answers FAQ

What is the difference between an accelerometer and a velocity sensor?

An accelerometer measures acceleration in g and suits medium and high speeds, while a velocity sensor gives mm/s and suits low and medium speeds. At 600 rpm, Metrix shows a 100 mV/g sensor giving only about 8 mV for 0.5 in/s peak.

It is one of the first vibration analysis questions and answers interviewers ask.

How to convert vibration velocity in mm/s to displacement in microns?

Divide peak velocity by 2πf, then double it for peak to peak. For 4.5 mm/s rms at 25 Hz, peak velocity is 6.36 mm/s.

Displacement is 2 × 6.36 ÷ 157.1 = 0.081 mm, which is 81 µm peak to peak.

What vibration level in mm/s is acceptable for a pump motor?

Under ISO 10816 part 3, a group 2 machine of 15 to 300 kW on a rigid foundation stays in zone B up to 2.8 mm/s rms. Zone C runs to 4.5 mm/s, and above that zone D means damage is likely.

Which frequency in the spectrum shows unbalance and which shows misalignment?

Unbalance shows mainly as a high radial 1X peak with low axial vibration. Misalignment shows a high axial 1X, a strong 2X peak, or both.

Phase helps separate them, because misalignment usually shifts phase across the coupling while unbalance keeps it steady.

How to calculate the outer race defect frequency of a bearing?

Use BPFO = (n ÷ 2) × shaft speed × (1 minus d ÷ D × cos θ). For a 6205 bearing with 9 balls, d of 7.94 mm and D of 39.04 mm at 25 Hz, BPFO is 89.6 Hz, or 3.58 times running speed.

Why do my vibration readings change every time I take them?

The usual cause is a different sensor spot, a different mounting or a change in load. Clips and hand held probes cut the usable frequency range compared with a stud.

Mark fixed points, mount the same way each time and record speed and load.
